title: Thanks to AI, we're all making browser games wild again
author: Donkeytonk
selftext:
I love seeing all the crazy stuff you guys are building. The odds are against us in so many ways but keep the faith, soon we're gonna show the world that browser games will matter again in a big way.

Anyways, a little update from my 100% vibe coded destruction-based beat smasher - more visual polish, better onboarding, new beat assist mode, free aim mode and more play-influenced procedural music (higher streaks add more chords and effects to smashes).

Any questions about my work flow or what's going on in the video, let me know below, happy to answer and give feedback on your own projects.

It does not follow from the premise that browser games have lower performance than games with a dedicated engine that the only reason that anyone would develop a browser game is having no knowledge of how to make games or use a game engine. For many types of game where performance is not critical (especially simpler games), the deployment and accessibility benefits of a browser game significantly outweigh any performance issues.

Obviously, it would be silly to try to write a performance critical game in a browser - but equally, it would be silly to use a complex high performance game engine rather than a browser to make a Solitaire clone.

replies.author: Robonotes1760
replies.body:
That's a non-sequitur: in other words, it is possible for the conclusion to be false even if all the premises are true. In other words, even if it is true that the only way that a person can deploy a game without specialist knowledge is via a web browser, it does not follow that everyone who can deploy other than a web browser would choose not to deploy through a web browser. As we have already discussed, there are advantages and disadvantages of both approaches and each individual game would need to be assessed as to what is most suitable. A first person shooter with realistic graphics, for example, is likely to be better developed using an existing engine such as Godot or UE5/6. A solitaire clone or point and click adventure, for example, would be more suited to a web browser. 

And also, the alternatives are not limited to web browser or third party game engine. There is also the important third category of non-browser games which do not use a third party game engine: in other words, the way that all games were made about 30 years ago and before. In the pre-AI days, I spent many years working on a fork of just such an open source game (a transport simulator from the 1990s), and modifying it such that it does actually require quite significant CPU and memory/memory bandwidth when played with very large maps. Obviously, that game would not be suitable for a browser environment as it relies on a legacy codebase and is performance critical, with lots of custom multi-threading architecture, memory management, etc.. 

But if the intention is to create a 1980s style platform game where the player plays as the antagonist and the protagonist is controlled by a computer, for example, as I did recently, then a browser deployment is optimum. The entire game, including oscillator sound effects and music, code-based graphics, and complex pathfinding for the protagonist, including a skill rating system that generates more mistakes at lower skill, fit into a single HTML file. 

Also, the more complex kind of games that require a game engine (or a complex independent codebase) are the sort that take a huge amount of time and effort to produce; that is fine for those whose full time job it is as game developers, or people with a very large amount of free time on their hands, but many people have full time jobs outside the games industry and would just like to create a nice straightforward game to enjoy in their spare time. People in that position may well intentionally choose the kind of game that is most suited to web browser development for that reason: but that does not mean that that kind of game would be better off if it were generated in an engine. 

The interesting consequence of AI is that it has moved the emphasis from implementation to design: but even designing a complex game is a very major endeavour. Without really enormous advances in AI from the current base line, large and complex games will still need very significant and in many cases professional level involvement. AI at current levels really does not do well with design and narrative generation, as opposed to technical implementation.

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
That’s not a lie. Roblox is one of the engines I’ve built on, started in the late 2010s, had plenty of success on the platform up to this year. 

The last game I solo built there was started mid 2025. It was my first title that was mostly vibe coded but still took more than half a year to see any success. 

Prior to that, I hand coded everything. I’m not a super advanced programmer but good enough to have built compelling games that that have had tens of millions of players.

I started building with Claude + threejs this year and able to experiment and iterate at a rate not possible as a solo dev, even with Claude hooked up to Roblox. It’s the Wild West right now, but I’m convinced threejs has changed the game.

comments.body: Okay but what is the actual gameplay here? I think vibecoders do not play games or have any vision. Is this fun or engaging in any way?

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
It’s a rhythm game where your fists make music as you smash through the level. Each material has a different instrumental sound so you’ll feel like your are playing music as you clear a level.

The more accurate your smashes, the higher the score you get. So you need to keep in rhythm to clear a level.

replies.author: LusikkaFeed
replies.body: So basically click in rhythm and make random noises

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
Not random noises, each note you make is in key with the chords and scales of a given bar of the music so you’ll feel like your jamming along to the track.

The higher streaks, the richer the sound becomes adding layers of chords and material-appropriate effects.

replies.author: LusikkaFeed
replies.body: Okay but the core concept is click in rhythm even if you have cherries on top. Is it fun? What is the gameplay loop?

replies.author: Donkeytonk
replies.body:
The core loop is you smash blocks to the rhythm to get musicoins, the more accurate you smash, the more musicoins you get from a block. If you string combos together, you release more musicoins per block. 

Harder blocks take more to smash but release more musicoins. Musicoims also double up as projectiles. 

Destroying structures with musicoin projectiles gives you bigger musicoin payouts but it’s harder to keep combos going when you fire musicoin projectiles, so there’s an element of risk/reward using them.

In a nutshell, if you play a level without being in rhythm, you won’t hit your musicoin goal. The more in rhythm you are, not only does it feel more fun (more visual and harmonic musical juice from the smashing), you will score higher, more likely to clear a level and can go for higher star awards.

Had about 1000 organic players in the last few weeks. Yesterday, average playtime in a session was about 20 minutes, pretty decent for a web browser game. Top 10% of players play up to an hour.
